specPoints.text: know and use the relationship between voltage, current and resistance: voltage = current × resistance V = I × R

primer.text: Every component, even a plain copper wire, pushes back a little against the current trying to pass through it. That push-back is resistance. This note defines the ohm, shows how resistance throttles the current at a fixed voltage, and assembles the equation linking voltage, current and resistance that solves most simple circuits.

lessons.title: Calculating current, resistance & potential difference
lessons.opening: Squeeze a garden hose and the flow drops; leave it open and the flow soars. Resistance does to charge exactly what your hand does to the water. This lesson defines the ohm, sets the see-saw between resistance and current, and assembles the equation V = I × R that ties all three quantities together.
keyPoints: Resistance describes how strongly a component opposes the flow of current through it.
Resistance is measured in ohm units (Ω); one ohm lets one volt drive one amp through a component.
For a fixed voltage, a higher resistance means a smaller current, and a lower resistance means a larger one.
The three quantities are linked by V = I × R.
Copper wiring has a very low resistance, which is why it counts as a good conductor.
In exam circuits the wires, ammeters and cells are taken to have zero resistance.

low.restatement: Resistance is the brake on the current: more ohms means less flow for the same push.
low.analogy: A narrow door in a busy corridor — the wider the door (lower resistance), the more people (current) get through.
low.examPointer: Use Ω for ohms in your working, and keep V, A and Ω labelled in every substitution.

medium.restatement: The equation is a see-saw: at fixed voltage, current and resistance move in opposite directions, because I = V ÷ R.
medium.analogy: A credit limit: the voltage is your budget, the resistance is the price of goods, and the current is how much you can buy.
medium.examPointer: Assume wires, ammeters and cells have zero resistance unless a question says otherwise — only the named components count.

options.explanation: Amperes measure current.
Volts measure voltage.
The ohm (Ω) is the unit of resistance.
Coulombs measure charge.

check.stem: A resistance of one ohm is equivalent to:

options.explanation: A 1 V push that drives a 1 A flow means the component has 1 Ω.
The causality runs voltage first, current second.
That defines a volt, not an ohm.
That defines an ampere, not an ohm.

check.stem: For the same voltage, doubling a component's resistance makes the current through it:

options.explanation: Current and resistance move oppositely at fixed voltage.
With V fixed, I = V ÷ R, so twice the resistance gives half the current.
The resistance sets the current, so changing it must change the flow.
Doubling is not blocking; some current still flows.

check.stem: A current of 0.3 A flows through a 10 Ω resistor. The voltage across it is:

options.explanation: That slips two decimal places: 0.3 × 10 = 3, not 30.
Adding the values is meaningless.
That divides current by resistance instead of multiplying.

check.stem: Copper is used for connecting wires because it has:

options.explanation: High resistance would choke the very current the wires exist to carry.
Copper is full of movable charge — that is the point.
A low-resistance metal lets current pass easily, so copper is a good conductor.

options.text: a resistance that grows as the current grows
options.explanation: That behaviour belongs to heating components like filaments, not copper wiring.

check.stem: Write down the equation linking voltage, current and resistance, naming the unit of each quantity.
check.modelAnswer: V = I × R, with voltage in volts, current in amperes and resistance in ohms.

check.stem: What happens to the current in a circuit if the resistance is increased while the voltage stays fixed?
check.modelAnswer: The current falls, because a higher resistance opposes the flow more strongly at the same voltage.

check.stem: Explain why a wire with a higher resistance carries a smaller current for the same voltage.
check.modelAnswer: Resistance opposes the drift of charge, so at a fixed voltage a larger resistance leaves less current — the two effects balance through V = I × R.

check.stem: A lamp draws 0.5 A from a 6 V supply. Calculate its resistance.

glossary.definition: The opposition a component offers to the current trying to flow through it, measured in ohms.
The unit of resistance — one volt driving one amp through the component.
A material that lets charge flow through it easily.
The rate at which electric charge streams through a component, measured in amperes.
The low-resistance metal usually chosen for connecting wires.

workedExample.prompt: Find the voltage across a 10 Ω resistor carrying a current of 0.3 A.
steps: List the knowns: resistance R = 10 Ω and current I = 0.3 A.
State the linking equation: V = I × R.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The voltage across the resistor is 3 V.
